cases.text: Ein Highlight unserer Tansania-Reise! Wir durften die Bohnen selbst über dem Feuer rösten, und der Duft war unbeschreiblich. Noor erzählt so lebendig von ihrem Leben als Kaffeebäuerin, dass man ihr ewig zuhören könnte. Mein Tipp: Verkauft doch die frisch gerösteten Bohnen zum Mitnehmen, ich hätte sofort drei Packungen als Mitbringsel gekauft.

ideas: sell roasted beans to take home

got.translation_en: A highlight of our Tanzania trip! We were allowed to roast the beans ourselves over the fire, and the aroma was indescribable. Noor tells so vividly about her life as a coffee farmer that you could listen to her forever. My tip: please sell the freshly roasted beans to take away; I would have immediately bought three packs as souvenirs.

cases.text: ヌールさんはとても親切で、コーヒーの話も勉強になりました。ただ、農園までの道がわかりにくく、緑の「Kahawa」の看板を見逃して何度も行き過ぎてしまいました。また、斜面の途中に日陰や休める場所がなく、午後の回は少しつらかったです。全体としては、良かった点と残念だった点が半々でした。

got.translation_en: Nuur-san was very kind, and I learned a lot from the coffee talk. However, the road to the farm was hard to find, and I missed the green 'Kahawa' sign and drove past it many times. Also, there was no shade or place to rest partway up the slope, so the afternoon session was a bit tough. Overall, the good points and the disappointing points were about half and half.

cases.text: We booked this tour on a whim while staying in Moshi and it ended up being the best day of our two weeks in Tanzania. Noor was a wonderful guide: she met us where the track ends and walked us up the slope between the coffee trees, explaining everything from picking to pulping to drying, and the views over the valley kept getting better. Lower down she showed us the maize and beans and told us about the cooperative she belongs to, which gave us a real sense of what a farming year looks like here. Then we roasted our own beans over a fire, which was the highlight for me, and drank the result: honestly the best cup of coffee I've had in years. The only hiccup was finding the place: the green Kahawa sign after the primary school is easy to miss and the dirt track beyond it looks like it leads nowhere. One idea: sell small bags of the roasted beans and maybe offer a few days at harvest time, because half our group wanted to take some home and the other half wanted to come back and pick.

Noor was a wonderful guide: she met us where the track ends and walked us up the slope between the coffee trees, explaining everything from picking to pulping to drying, and the views over the valley kept getting better. Lower down she showed us the maize and beans and told us about the cooperative she belongs to, which gave us a real sense of what a farming year looks like here. Then we roasted our own beans over a fire, which was the highlight for me, and drank the result: honestly the best cup of coffee I've had in years. The only hiccup was finding the place: the green Kahawa sign after the primary school is easy to miss and the dirt track beyond it looks like it leads nowhere. One idea: sell small bags of the roasted beans and maybe offer a few days at harvest time, because half our group wanted to take some home and the other half wanted to come back and pick.
